rv.q: This haunted, surreally comic, tender heartbreaker of a play is about what happens when the thing you want so badly that it stalks your dreams slips out of reach.
Oh, the fallacy of thinking that just because something hurts, it is profound.
It’s a stunning visual feast, and an arresting theatre experience.
It's one of the season's more striking performances so far.
Onwunali navigates Udofia’s complex text with marvelous lucidity and emotional range.
Through a Nigerian American mythic lens, Mfoniso Udofia’s personal play is a chronicle of health, writer’s block, and self-care, but it doesn't explore all these themes deeply enough.
Stretches of Udofia’s complex, often lyrical, modern-day drama escaped me entirely.
Udofia has sent the invitation, regardless of your own lived experience. I suggest you open it.

Magical, surreal, and breathtaking, creation stories and all the important importants encapsulates this journey in a hug of Nigerian culture and classical music, offering many relatable moments along the way.
Onwunali makes the challenge of realizing them riveting.

The story Udofia has written is emotionally potent—when I described it afterward to my wife, a psychologist, she said the ideas and themes would powerfully resonate with many of her clients—but it is not fully realized in its current form, despite the imaginative way in which it is told.
There’s also a good deal of predictability in Creation Stories.

cn.t: Udofia's ambitious IVF drama blending Nigerian mythology with modern pressures earns praise for Onwunali's transfixing performance and inventive structure, though some critics find its maximalist style exhausting.

vr.q: Unfortunately, I was bored during this play because I just wasn't invested enough in this character.
